articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions Iranian Shadow Banking Networks in Sweeping 'Operation Economic Outcast'
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed sanctions on over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel. This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aims to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks, which are used to move billions of dollars through the international financial system despite comprehensive sanctions.

The sanctioned entities include Iranian exchange houses and overseas trading companies, primarily based in Dubai, with others in Hong Kong and Turkey, that facilitate payments for Iranian oil, petrochemical, and metals exporters.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that Iran's economy is 'underwater' and its leaders are 'panicking,' calling the shadow banking system the 'last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime.' The action was taken pursuant to Executive Orders 13902, 13224 (as amended), and 13871, targeting Iran's financial, counter-terrorism, and metals sectors, respectively.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designations and New Cuba Frequently Asked Questions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations and the issuance of Cuba Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). The Iran designations are part of ongoing efforts to target illicit financial activities supporting the Iranian regime.

While specific details of the Iran designations were not immediately available in the summary, the issuance of Cuba FAQs indicates a continued focus on clarifying and enforcing sanctions related to Cuba.

The U.S. has maintained a comprehensive system of sanctions against Cuba for decades, with recent measures intensifying the 'maximum-pressure campaign' and impacting humanitarian access to essential goods and services.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations; Amends Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations related to counter narcotics and cyber-related activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit networks involved in drug trafficking and malicious cyber operations.
In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions related to illicit drugs.

Additionally, an amended Russia-related General License and associated Frequently Asked Questions were released, indicating adjustments to existing sanctions against Russia. This comes as the EU also continues to expand its sanctions against Russia, targeting various sectors including financial services and energy.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has implemented new counter terrorism designations. These designations target individuals and entities identified as supporting or engaging in terrorist activities.

The specific details of the individuals and entities designated were not immediately available in the summary. However, such actions are a routine part of the U.S. government's efforts to combat global terrorism by disrupting financial and material support networks.
These designations fall under OFAC's broader mandate to administer and enforce U.S. sanctions programs aimed at protecting national security and foreign policy interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting both counter narcotics and counter terrorism efforts. This dual focus highlights the interconnected nature of these illicit activities and the U.S. government's comprehensive approach to combating them.
These designations aim to disrupt the financial and operational networks of individuals and organizations involved in drug trafficking and terrorist financing.
The actions underscore OFAC's commitment to leveraging its sanctions authorities to protect the U.S. financial system from abuse by criminal and terrorist organizations.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has released an update regarding Iran designations. This update likely involves modifications to existing listings or additional information concerning previously sanctioned individuals or entities.
Such updates are a regular part of OFAC's sanctions programs, ensuring that the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List and other sanctions lists remain current and accurate.
The ongoing Iran sanctions program targets various sectors of the Iranian economy and individuals involved in activities deemed destabilizing or illicit by the U.S. government.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations. These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to exert economic pressure on Iran.
The designations aim to disrupt financial networks and other avenues used by the Iranian regime to fund its activities.
Previous Iran-related sanctions have targeted various sectors, including oil, petrochemicals, and metals, as well as individuals and entities involved in sanctions evasion.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Imposes Cuba Designations and Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to combat illicit financial flows and disruptive cyber operations globally.

In a significant move concerning Cuba, OFAC also imposed new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination. This determination makes foreign firms operating in Cuba's electronics, manufacturing, marine, or technology sectors liable to U.S. sanctions.

Eight companies and two individuals were designated, and five Cuban-flagged tankers were identified as blocked property, linking them to Cuba's fuel shipping, state companies, ruling elite, and military supply. This expands on Executive Order 14404 of May 1, 2026, which broadened the scope of U.S. sanctions targeting Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-related Designations and Venezuela-related General License Amendment
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to address activities deemed contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
In conjunction with these actions, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert, likely providing guidance or warnings regarding specific illicit activities or evasion tactics.

Additionally, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question were issued. This General License 5AA further delays the effectiveness of the authorization in GL 5 until December 18, 2026, impacting transactions related to the sale or transfer of CITGO shares in connection with the PdVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment likely modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are issued by OFAC to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. Amendments can expand, narrow, or clarify the scope of these authorizations.
This action reflects OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions implementation, adjusting regulations as needed to achieve policy objectives while potentially mitigating unintended consequences.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
